1395.bp: When you search on Amazon or eBay for 'shoes,' the engine needs to know you mean shoes-the-product, not shoe-repair or shoe-reviews, so it can show you the right category of items and organize the page sensibly. This is called query classification: taking what a person typed and deciding which bucket it belongs in.
1395.wh: Real e-commerce systems have thousands of categories, and shoppers almost always ask about popular ones (running shoes, boots, heels) rather than obscure ones (orthopedic shoe inserts for diabetics). Traditional classifiers are like a student who memorizes the popular answers and flails on anything rare. Also, new categories emerge all the time—once the system ships, you cannot just retrain it on thousands of new labels. You need a way to handle a brand new category label the moment someone creates it.
1395.ap: Instead of memorizing which queries historically went with which categories, the paper treats categories like people: each has a profile—a rich description of what it means. A query like 'waterproof hiking boots' and a category like 'waterproof hiking footwear for outdoor expeditions' are now scored by their semantic similarity—how much they mean the same thing—rather than by looking up whether that exact phrase has appeared before. This lets a rare query find the right category even if nobody has ever asked it before.
1395.ww: This works because meaning and co-occurrence are different things. A query and a category might have never appeared together in historical data, but if their descriptions are semantically aligned—if they literally talk about the same thing—then they belong together. For a brand new category, the system just reads its description and immediately understands which queries it should serve.
1395.po: The paper shows their system beats existing methods and, crucially, handles rare queries better than the traditional approach. It also solves the 'zero-shot' problem: add a new category description to the system, and it starts working immediately, without retraining on thousands of examples.

1396.bp: When you search Spotify for '70s funk,' the system shows you songs and playlists. Someone (a human or an automated judge) must decide whether those results are actually good—whether they match what you were looking for. At massive scale and in many languages, paying humans to rate millions of searches is impossible, so companies are starting to use large language models as automated judges.
1396.wh: Language models are powerful but they can hallucinate: they reason based on world knowledge and semantic similarity, but they may not know how *real users actually behaved* on this exact search. If a search is ambiguous—say, 'Paris' could mean the city or the person—the model might confidently rate an irrelevant result as good just because it's written well. Worse, in different languages and cultural contexts, user intent drifts.
1396.ap: The paper teaches the language model to be a judge that cites its reasoning. For each search result shown, it creates a small 'evidence card' that says: 'Here's how users actually clicked on similar searches and results in the past.' When the model sees these cards, it can now say 'I think this result is good because (1) semantic reasoning says X, and (2) real users clicked similar results in the past.' The model learns to use both signals together.
1396.ww: Ambiguity needs ground truth, not just logic. If I ask about 'Paris' and you can say 'real people who searched for

clicked this fashion link 500 times,' that's evidence worth citing. The model, which is trained to explain itself, naturally learns to trust evidence over pure reasoning when they conflict, and that makes its judgments stick closer to what real people actually wanted.
1396.po: On Spotify searches, this approach improved alignment with user preferences by 5% overall, and by 91% on tricky, disagreement-heavy cases. On multi-language datasets, it boosted accuracy by another 15%, showing that historical user behavior transcends language and helps clarify intent.

1397.bp: AI systems now answer questions by finding relevant text on the web and citing where they got the information—like how a lawyer cites case law. But AI answer engines only cite a handful of sources. If your website is mentioned but not cited, users never see it. The question is: what makes a source get cited first?
1397.wh: This is a new kind of competition. In traditional search, websites competed on ranking (position in results). Now they must compete on being cited—and the rules are different. Being ranked number one does not guarantee you get cited; the AI might pick a different source. Understanding what makes a source 'citable' is opaque because it depends on how the language model reasons, not just on keyword matches.
1397.ap: The paper builds a clean experiment: show the language model exactly two sources that differ in only one way—say, one has 'buy for $19.99' and the other does not—and count which one gets cited first. They repeated this 252,000 times, trying different factors like relevance, price, date, trust signals, and formatting. They also shuffled source order to make sure the AI was not just picking whichever came first.
1397.ww: By isolating one factor at a time, you can see which ones actually matter in the model's reasoning. Topical relevance and position came out as the strongest drivers; price and recency also help. But pure formatting (bolding, layout) barely moves the needle. This tells you what the language model actually 'cares' about when deciding to cite something, rather than guessing.
1397.po: The paper gives practitioners a ranked checklist: optimize for these factors in this order. They tested it at Sprinklr (a marketing platform) and teams found it actionable. This work opens a new field—Generative Engine Optimization—which is now as real as traditional search optimization, but with different rules.

1398.bp: E-commerce search uses a multi-stage funnel: first, retrieve the most likely products; then pre-rank them to narrow the list; then rank them by relevance; finally, apply business rules. Pre-ranking is the speed bottleneck. It must be fast enough to handle millions of users without making the page slow, but smart enough to cut out irrelevant results before expensive ranking kicks in.
1398.wh: The challenge is that user behavior is sparse and diverse. Most users only browse a handful of items, so the system has little data to learn from. Also, a single user might search for completely different things (tennis rackets one day, kitchen sinks the next), so their behavior does not paint a coherent picture. Finally, pre-ranking is so latency-critical that even small computations add up across millions of simultaneous searches.
1398.ap: The paper splits user behavior into two streams: one capturing strong signals (items they clicked recently) and one capturing weak signals (items they browsed but did not engage). They compress each stream into fine-grained chunks, then use an attention mechanism that does not compute pairwise comparisons between all chunks—instead, it computes a single score per query. This reduces computational complexity from O(N) to O(1), meaning the cost does not grow with the number of items. They also add a mechanism to move knowledge from high-volume categories (lots of data) to sparse categories (little data).
1398.ww: By separating strong and weak signals, the system can weight them differently: strong signals are crisp and recent, weak signals are noisy but reveal broader interest. By compressing these into chunks and using query-centric scoring, the system avoids the quadratic blowup that would kill latency. And by transferring learned patterns from popular categories to rare ones, it bootstraps intelligence in sparse regions.
1398.po: The paper shows a 36% latency reduction and significant accuracy gains. More importantly, they deployed it in a live large-scale e-commerce system, proving it works under real load. Users see faster search results without losing quality.

1399.bp: E-commerce sellers need search to return their products when customers search. But simple keyword matching fails on complex searches like 'waterproof jacket that breathes for winter hiking.' Modern language models can reason through these queries brilliantly, but they are slow—each answer takes 100+ milliseconds because the model generates text token by token. In real-time search, that is unacceptable.
1399.wh: Knowledge distillation (teaching a small model from a large one) is the usual answer, but it forces a brutal trade-off: either you keep the large model's reasoning ability and lose interpretability, or you make a small fast model but destroy the reasoning. And if you try to preserve reasoning by forcing a human to write out the reasoning steps for every training example, the cost becomes astronomical.
1399.ap: The paper proposes a three-step pipeline. First, they fine-tune a large language model teacher using only binary labels (relevant or not) and a reward signal that pushes the model to improve its reasoning—specifically, the reasoning should help predict relevance. The model learns to generate step-by-step reasoning without requiring human annotations. Second, they train the model to score items with a single token output (no lengthy reasoning), keeping the internal reasoning alive for interpretability. Third, they transfer both the reasoning and the scoring ability to a 0.6B parameter student model through a specialized form of knowledge distillation.
1399.ww: By using only binary labels and task-aligned rewards, the system avoids the annotation cost. By decoupling reasoning from ranking (reasoning inside, single-score output), it becomes fast and deployable. By distilling both aspects together, the small model retains the 'why' of its decisions, not just the 'what.'
1399.po: A tiny 0.6B student model achieves comparable accuracy to much larger models, generates step-by-step reasoning users can see, and runs fast enough for production search. This bridges the gap between interpretability and speed that previously seemed impossible.

1400.bp: Search engines rank items, but the language model behind the ranking has a weird bias: it pays too much attention to the first document, almost regardless of relevance. This is called 'attention sink drift'—the model's internal mechanism gets stuck on early items. In production search serving billions of queries, this bias kills accuracy and forces teams to run expensive calibration after ranking, which halves throughput.
1400.wh: The bias is structural: in standard transformer models, the first token naturally accumulates weight during the computation. Engineers assumed this was baked into the model architecture and could only be fixed by recalibrating results after ranking. Recalibration works but is painfully slow because you must rank all candidates first, then reprocess them.
1400.ap: The paper proposes training the model differently so it fixes its own bias without needing post-processing. During training, they use a special attention head designed to suppress background noise and highlight retrieval heads (the parts that actually care about relevance). They also introduce a new training objective that aligns attention weights with semantic importance—if a document is relevant, the model learns to attend to it; if it is not, the model learns to ignore it.
1400.ww: By moving the calibration into training, the model learns to overcome its positional bias during inference, without any extra computation. The attention heads learn to differentiate between 'document at position 1' and 'actually relevant document,' so position does not trick the model.
1400.po: Deployed at WeChat (over 1 billion users), the method achieved a 3.3x latency speedup (down to 26.56ms), improved engagement metrics like click-through rate by 0.4%, and boosted user satisfaction by 1.25%—all while running much faster than the old recalibration approach.

1401.bp: Advertising platforms need to generate lots of different headlines for ads so they do not bore or annoy users by showing the same message over and over. But language models have a tendency to converge on a few popular patterns (they call this 'mode collapse')—they generate the same handful of headlines repeatedly, defeating the purpose of using machine generation.
1401.wh: A large language model trained on diverse ad data still learns that certain words and structures appear most often in successful ads, so it gravitate toward repeating those patterns. Diversity techniques like random sampling can produce varied output but often make the headlines incoherent or irrelevant. You are trapped: chase diversity and lose quality; chase quality and lose diversity.
1401.ap: The paper builds an end-to-end training system that explicitly optimizes for multiple goals at once. First, they create high-quality training pairs synthetically—different variations of ad descriptions and desired outcomes. Second, they use reinforcement learning to train the model to balance three objectives: diversity (generate different headlines), faithfulness (headlines match the product), and business metrics (predict clicks). The model learns to optimize all three simultaneously, not one at a time.
1401.ww: By explicitly optimizing for diversity as a learned objective—not as a sampling trick—the model internalizes diversity as part of what it means to be a good ad headline generator. The reinforcement learning signal tells it: 'If you generate the same headline twice, that is bad; if you generate varied coherent headlines, that is good.' Unlike sampling-based tricks, this shapes the model's learned behavior.
1401.po: On Xiaohongshu (a major platform), the deployed system increased advertiser value by 4% and click-through rate by 1.4% compared to previous approaches. Users saw more varied ads, advertisers got better results—a win on both sides.

1402.bp: E-commerce products have two faces: a title and an image. A query like 'blue waterproof jacket' might match the image perfectly but the title might just say 'All-Weather Jacket' (vague marketing speak). Real relevance ranking must understand both modalities and figure out which parts of the query are answered by the image versus the text. But language models that can reason through this are too slow for production ranking.
1402.wh: Existing methods either ignore one modality or treat title and image as separate signals without fine-grained reasoning. A language model can reason through which query terms are answered by the image and which by the title, but it takes 100+ milliseconds per item. A small fast model cannot do this reasoning. The gap between capability and speed is the problem.
1402.ap: The paper trains a large language model to reason step-by-step about which query terms each modality satisfies, using chain-of-thought reasoning guided by rewards based on term coverage. This reasoning happens once during training, offline. Then they distill this reasoning into a small, fast model using a specialized distillation strategy that forces the small model to inherit the term-level reasoning logic, not just memorize outputs.
1402.ww: By using chain-of-thought rewards, the language model learns to generate fine-grained reasoning that mirrors the actual reasoning needed for ranking. By distilling at the term level, the small model learns to replicate that reasoning pattern, so it can apply the same logic to new queries and products at serving time.
1402.po: A small model inherits the large model's ability to reason about multi-modal relevance term-by-term and can execute this reasoning at production speed. Offline experiments show significant improvements; online deployment would confirm the real-world lift.

1403.bp: Apps like TikTok, YouTube, and Reddit increasingly have built-in chatbots that suggest topics to users ('Want to talk about?'). The chatbot needs to suggest topics the user will actually engage with. But the vast majority of user data is about videos or content they consumed, not conversations they had. How do you recommend conversation topics when you have little conversation data?
1403.wh: There is a domain gap: preferences revealed by content consumption (what videos you watched) are not the same as preferences revealed by conversation (what you talk about). Watching a makeup tutorial does not mean you want to chat about makeup tips. If you try to directly apply the content preferences to topic recommendation, you get poor suggestions. But if you only use the scarce conversation data, you do not have enough signal to learn anything reliable.
1403.ap: The paper proposes a two-stage framework. First, they learn how to adapt user content preferences to the conversation domain—they identify what aspects of content preference transfer and what aspects differ. Second, they align these adapted preferences to the user's real-time context—what they are doing *right now*. For example, if someone just finished a cooking video, the system might suggest cooking-related topics, but only if the user is in a conversational mood right now.
1403.ww: By explicitly modeling the domain gap and learning how to bridge it, the system leverages the abundant content data (lots of video watches) to bootstrap understanding in the sparse domain (few conversation starts). The real-time alignment layer ensures suggestions feel contextual, not random.
1403.po: Deployed on a large-scale application, the system significantly improved chatbot engagement—more users clicked the suggested topics and started conversations. This shows the domain-transfer approach actually works at scale.

1404.bp: E-commerce search ranking depends on knowing whether a product is truly relevant to a query. Language models are phenomenal at reasoning about this, but they need context (product description, reviews, specifications) to make good decisions. If that context is noisy or wrong, the model becomes confused. Also, production systems have strict latency budgets—there is no time for multiple passes or refinement.
1404.wh: External knowledge (product descriptions, reviews, specs) is often noisy, stale, or contradictory. A product description might claim a item is 'waterproof' but customer reviews say it leaks. A language model cannot easily tell which source to trust, especially when it has a strict time limit and no room for follow-up reasoning. It must make a simultaneous decision about both relevance and context trustworthiness in a single forward pass.
1404.ap: The paper uses reinforcement learning to teach the model to learn which context to trust and which to ignore. During training, they show the model two versions: one with external context, one without. By comparing how much better the model's decision becomes with context, they teach it a 'trust signal'—a number that says 'this context is worth using' or 'this context is misleading, ignore it.' This happens within a single inference pass using structured chain-of-thought reasoning.
1404.ww: By training on both contexts and comparing them during learning, the model learns empirically which context matters and which does not, without needing a human to label 'this context is trustworthy.' The structured reasoning format keeps the decision transparent and fast.
1404.po: Deployed in Taobao (hundreds of millions of users), the system improved ranking accuracy on query slices with noisy context, particularly for long-tail queries where external knowledge is sparse or contradictory. A single-pass inference architecture delivers these gains without added latency.

1405.bp: Job search starts with vague queries: most people search with three words or fewer ('senior software engineer'). The system needs to infer intent (What industry? What company size? Remote or on-site?) and suggest refinements interactively. At scale, these suggestions must be fast, personalized, and accurate.
1405.wh: A three-word query is massively ambiguous. 'Senior software engineer' could mean embedded systems, web development, machine learning, or finance. The system could ask the user to filter by category, but building a rigid taxonomy of all possible filters is tedious and breaks when new job types emerge. Also, suggestions must arrive in milliseconds during live search.
1405.ap: The paper proposes a ranking pipeline for real-time facet (attribute) suggestions. First, they curate a taxonomy of job attributes offline (company size, industry, remote status, seniority, etc.). Then at query time, they use embedding-based retrieval to find candidate facets (say, top 20 candidates for what the user might care about), and rank them with a small language model. The model is distilled to run with minimal latency—single-token scoring and batch prefixing to enable fast serving.
1405.ww: By separating taxonomy curation (offline, strategic) from retrieval (candidate generation) and scoring (fast, learned ranking), the system avoids the rigidity of hand-crafted rules while staying fast. Embedding retrieval quickly filters candidates, and the small language model does precision ranking.
1405.po: Online A/B testing showed significant lifts in suggestion engagement and downstream job search outcomes. The system helps job seekers refine vague queries into concrete searches and find better matches faster.

1406.bp: LinkedIn has millions of job postings, each messy and unstructured—some are one paragraph, some ramble, some use marketing jargon instead of standard job terminology. The system must convert these into standardized fields (required skills, seniority level, job category, etc.) to power search, recommendations, and recruiter tools. This is called 'job understanding,' and it must work at massive scale.
1406.wh: Job postings are written by humans with no template, so they use different words for the same concept. One posting lists 'Python' and another says 'coding in Python.' A small language model struggles with this variability. A large one could handle it but is too slow to run on millions of postings. Also, new job types and attributes emerge constantly, so the system needs to generalize beyond its training data.
1406.ap: The paper trains a small language model (not a giant one) using two strategies. First, they create synthetic training tasks that combine two modes: taxonomy-guided classification (if the posting mentions 'C++,' label it as 'programming language') and taxonomy-agnostic entity extraction (find any mention of required skills, even if they are not in the taxonomy). Second, they add reasoning traces—step-by-step explanations—to the synthetic data, so the model learns not just to memorize but to explain its decisions. Finally, they use multi-adapter architecture, so different downstream tasks (extracting skills vs. extracting company size) have specialized parameters but share the main model.
1406.ww: By combining classification and extraction, the model learns structured understanding in both directions: 'fit into known buckets' and 'surface new information.' Reasoning traces teach the model to generalize beyond exact matches. Multi-adapters let each task specialize without fragmenting the model into separate systems.
1406.po: Offline and online A/B tests show significant improvements in accuracy and operational simplicity. LinkedIn's teams report easier model management and better generalization to new job types.

1407.bp: E-commerce search ranking depends on product descriptions, but many descriptions are long and verbose, padded with marketing speak. For ranking in real-time with a cross-encoder architecture (a model that looks at query + product together), passing the full description is computationally expensive. The system needs concise, query-relevant summaries to rank fast without sacrificing accuracy.
1407.wh: A summary is only useful if it highlights the parts relevant to the query. Generic summaries miss crucial details. But generating query-specific summaries during ranking is slow. If you pre-compute summaries without knowing the query, they are not optimized for ranking. There is no way to know what summary will help ranking most without running ranking itself.
1407.ap: The paper proposes using reinforcement learning to generate summaries offline that are optimized for downstream ranking. The process: generate a summary of the product (using only product information, not the query), then use that summary in ranking and measure how well it ranks relevant items. The ranking quality becomes the reward signal during summary generation. This trains the model to generate summaries that, even without seeing the query, highlight ranking-critical information.
1407.ww: By using ranking accuracy as the reward, the summary generation process learns what matters for ranking. The generated summaries might never mention the query directly, but they unconsciously emphasize the attributes that most queries care about (e.g., size, color, durability, warranty).
1407.po: Summaries can be generated and cached before any query arrives, so there is zero latency overhead at serving time. In online A/B tests, ReLSum improved user engagement metrics like orders per visitor by meaningful margins, proving that smarter summaries actually help people find products better.

1408.bp: Companies operate in their own industries with specialized language and domain knowledge. A telecom company needs to understand customer opinions about specific services (5G quality, customer support, competitor strengths) from messy forum posts and reviews. Large language models are powerful but they are trained on general internet text, not telecom jargon. How do you adapt them to vertical domains cheaply?
1408.wh: Adapting a language model to a new domain usually means pretraining it on domain data (continuous pretraining), then fine-tuning on specific tasks. But continuous pretraining is expensive in compute and often does not help much when the base model is already strong. For low-resource languages like Traditional Chinese, it is even harder. The usual approach wastes time and money.
1408.ap: The paper tests this empirically with Chunghwa Telecom. They adapt three open-source models (LLaMA-3, Qwen, Mistral) for the specific task of extracting structured opinions from unstructured forum discussions. Their main finding: continuous pretraining on domain data provides little benefit when you already have a strong instruction-tuned model. Instead, they focus on high-quality instruction fine-tuning (training on specific tasks with human-written examples) and strategic data curation.
1408.ww: Strong instruction-tuned models already know how to follow directions and reason, so they rapidly adapt to a new domain when given clear task examples. Continuous pretraining tries to teach them new words and concepts, but that is redundant if they can already generalize from a few task examples.
1408.po: The paper provides practitioners actionable guidance: skip the expensive continuous pretraining step and invest in quality instruction examples instead. This significantly reduces the cost and time to deploy domain-adapted models in low-resource settings.

1409.bp: E-commerce search relies on embedding-based retrieval: the system converts queries and products into numerical vectors (embeddings) and finds the nearest neighbors. This is fast and scalable to billions of items. But as systems grow, the quality of these embeddings matters more—a query embedding that does not match product embeddings well means wrong results.
1409.wh: There are two gaps. First, the model is trained on narrow datasets (say, 100,000 products) but must retrieve from 100 million. The training optimized the model against a small set of competitors per query, not against the full corpus. Second, as companies upgrade to better models (say, from DistilBERT to GTE), they cannot just swap the old embeddings for new ones without disrupting the retrieval logic—the new embeddings might rank items in completely different orders.
1409.ap: The paper proposes two solutions deployed at Walmart. First, they improve training signals: instead of mining hard negatives (difficult false matches) only offline, they add online cross-batch sampling during training, which finds hard negatives in real-time from millions of products. They combine this with offline mining using a cross-encoder (a more sophisticated ranker) and metadata heuristics. Second, they transition to a better model using 'warm-start distillation': the new model learns from the old model's embeddings and decisions, ensuring the new model inherits domain-specific expertise from its predecessor.
1409.ww: By increasing the diversity and difficulty of negatives seen during training, the model learns a richer embedding space. By distilling from the old model during transition, the new model does not start from scratch—it bootstraps on the old model's knowledge and gradually improves.
1409.po: The unified pipeline scales embedding quality without disrupting retrieval. Extensive offline and online experiments validate the approach, showing improvements in retrieval precision and seamless model transitions.
